speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am going to start with a story about a land quite far away.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Civic Science, a US market research company, posed an innocent question in mid-2019.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Arabic numerals are the standard system for counting that we all use today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is based on 10 digits, including zero.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The name is a misnomer because the numbering system actually originates in India.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It reached Europe around the 10th century after further being developed in the Middle East, hence the term Arabic numerals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But many Americans have no idea what Arabic numerals are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They just know that they do not like the sound of it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: People do not always understand the things that they oppose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The debate on immigration is often driven by systematic mis-perceptions of who immigrants are, what they are doing in host countries and how they are contributing to the societies that they live in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Stephanie Stantcheva at Harvard and her colleagues studied perceptions of immigrants and social policy across six Western countries: France, Germany, Italy, Sweden, the UK and the US.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of asking people whether they like immigrants, she asks them for their best estimates of facts about immigration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, she asks people: what is the share of immigrants in your country?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This allows for a comparison between beliefs and reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Even if you added illegal immigrants and the native-born children of immigrants, you would not get anywhere near that estimate of one in three.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They think that immigrants are less educated, more likely to be unemployed and more likely to receive welfare benefits than they are in fact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The immigration debate in these countries appears to be deeply tainted by systematic bias against immigrants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is a very destructive narrative of a culturally, ethnically, religiously different immigrant, who has arrived in overwhelming numbers and is a welfare burden on the host society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This in turn poisons the policy debate not just on immigration but also on domestic social policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: People cannot think about questions like welfare reform and taxes without thinking about whether immigrants could benefit more than locals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Could we just tell people the truth about immigration?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Stantcheva also looked at whether presenting targeted facts on immigration to respondents helped to correct their mis-perceptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, it turns out that facts are not well absorbed, possibly because our biases are even stronger.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Respondents who read a short story about the struggles of a working-class immigrant improved their perception of immigrants and were less likely to think that immigrants were poor because of their own failings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We know that we are an immigrant society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That does not make us any less of a real country or a real people bound together as one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What it means is that being Singaporean is not permanently linked to any language – Singlish aside – or to history or ethnicity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have the room as a society for our identity to evolve with each new generation of Singaporeans, local-born and immigrants, together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We have the chance to define and to work towards becoming a better version of ourselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But each wave of immigration to Singapore has had both disruptive and productive effects on our economy and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the lifetime of our first generation of leaders, immigration swung from being a problem in a new country with high unemployment, a booming population and no natural resources to becoming the solution to a rapidly ageing society with manpower constraints and stagnant population growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Like many societies, we have developed a conflicted attitude towards immigration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We seek low-wage immigrants to do the dirty, dangerous, demanding jobs that we do not want to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We depend on high-wage immigrants to fulfill crucial skills shortages to make our economy more competitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we often prefer that immigrants are neither seen nor heard, that they fulfill their roles quietly and efficiently, without getting in our way or without competing for our jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We complain about immigrants refusing to integrate when it is not clear that we ourselves think that they can become Singaporean one day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We forget that sometimes, that we should never treat other people as solutions to our economic and social problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But let me get back to the problem of facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What do we actually know about the labour market for citizens?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How does it compare to that of more recent immigrants such as Permanent Residents (PRs)?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This question was debated in Parliament earlier this year because our labour market statistics cover residents as a whole and not citizens and PRs separately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, because citizens are the majority, this also means any differences between resident data and citizen data actually implies a much larger difference between citizens and PRs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Since PR data was not detailed in the MOM report, I will first compute it and then discuss it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Let us suppose that residents earn $10 an hour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is roughly the actual ratio of citizen-to-resident median earnings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, I want to find out how much PRs earn.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Out of every 10 residents, let us say eight are citizens, two are PRs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is lower than the real proportion but it makes the math a bit easier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, there are four citizens for each PR.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That means average earnings of citizens counts for four times as much as the average earnings of a PR when you compute the average earnings of residents overall.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is a $0.50 difference between citizen and resident earnings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: You multiply that by four times, you get $2.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That is actually the difference between PR and resident earnings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, in the example I gave, if a citizen earns $9.50 an hour, and residents earn $10 an hour, PRs must earn $12 an hour, $2 more than what residents do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Your real difference is actually a bit bigger because there is actually about 5.66 citizens to one PR in the labour force.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The point is if residents perform a bit better than citizens, actually, PRs are doing a lot better, much better, because PRs are a very small fraction of all residents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But that is because PRs are generally of prime working age, where the employment rate is high in any case, unlike citizens who are spread throughout all ages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I estimate that over the last decade about 71% of employed PRs were PMETs, and this did not change much over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While citizens have become substantially more skilled over time, PRs have always been fairly high-skilled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is difficult to estimate because median wages are reported, not average wages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But, take that figure with a grain of salt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The answer is no, not relative to citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: On average, a citizen is just above half as likely as a PR to be retrenched.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The citizen retrenchment estimate would go up if you assume that 10% of citizens are self-employed, but not by so much as to cover this gap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My estimates suggest PRs are more skilled, earn more, but also face more economic risks than citizens as they are much more likely to be retrenched.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There is little surprising about the first few points I made because PRs are often granted based on economic criteria.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If our selection of PRs is good, it is logical that they are going to do better on average in the labour market than citizens do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But reality is a bit more nuanced than we think.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The last point on retrenchment is, to me, surprising and needs further study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Most economists would argue the net effect of immigration is positive for the Singapore economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is that the net effect may hide substantial redistribution to the incomes and wealth of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some Singaporeans will have skills that are complemented by immigration and will have better job opportunities and wages, but others may see their job prospects harmed by competition for jobs that immigrants are also highly skilled in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Many Singaporeans also own assets ranging from property to stakes in businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These too benefit from immigration, so it affects wealth and not just the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the absence of credible research and readily accessible data, I fear that the destructive narratives about the quality and character of immigrants that now plagues politics in many Western countries, will also find a foothold in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Respondents also felt strongly that immigrants were not doing enough to integrate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Close to 40% of respondents felt that immigration issues, if mismanaged, could lead to communal anger; a decreased sense of national identity; and a fall in trust in Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There was, moreover, broad support for increased Government intervention to address immigration issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What might a successful Government intervention look like?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are distributional consequences of immigration and despite our best efforts at calibrating immigration flows and manpower policy, some Singaporeans will be better off and some worse off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We need research that documents how immigrants have contributed to our economy, as well as how immigrants have affected employment prospects and outcomes of locals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We need to understand who among our immigrants decides to put down roots in Singapore and who does not stay, and how they assimilate over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And we need to be prepared to grant targeted help to locals whom we discover are adversely affected by immigration, because the net positives of immigration for the country do not mean anything if your own livelihood is affected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While we cannot address systematic misperceptions about immigrants with facts alone, the facts are a good starting point.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But above all, we should not fall into the trap of thinking that the purpose of immigration is to solve the problem of our unwanted jobs, or our falling workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Nor does it make sense to think of immigration as simply a means of preserving the status quo and demographics of what Singapore is today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These ways of thinking are counter-productive and unworthy of an immigrant society because they treat immigrants merely as means, and not as an end.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I must add that I really admire his mental acrobatics and also confess that coming right after a Supplementary Budget presentation filled with very large numbers, I feel my head spinning a bit but I am not unwell; I can do this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This Government is focused not just on the present but on building a future of opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Because of our low birth rates and ageing, we face serious challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over the longer term, we aim for a stable and sustainable population.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our immigration policy does not serve just economic objectives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Applicants who can make good economic contributions are certainly welcome, but that is not the sole criterion we consider.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many of our new Permanent Residents (PR) and citizens have family ties with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most have lived here for many years, formed friendships with locals and are active in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: From an integration standpoint, these ties are very valuable and we cannot put a number to it easily, we cannot quantify it through any simple metric.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Assoc Prof Theseira pointed out that PRs generally have higher incomes and qualifications than existing citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the first place, that may be a rather narrow way to think of the PRs and to characterise them, and, really, not at all what we set out to achieve.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As I pointed out earlier, we prioritise those with the ability to integrate well into our society and who have expressed their longer term commitment to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If that were so, Assoc Prof Theseira, or anyone else, might well ask, quite legitimately, why we are taking in Permanent Residents, or residents who are not as well qualified as Singaporeans or were not doing as well as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, this debate would not end no matter how much research we do and no matter how much facts and data we put out.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We do actually have foreigners working in Singapore who generally earn less and are not as well qualified as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They are here on work passes and do not have long-term residency rights.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While we do take in a calibrated number of PRs and new citizens, we are first and foremost focused on improving citizens’ lives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is a very broad spectrum of things we do to uplift our people and that includes raising educational attainment and growing incomes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our people have shown consistently that when given the opportunities, they are willing to make the effort and they do well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If while we improve our own educational attainments and incomes, we also manage to attract people with good qualifications and incomes to join our Singapore family as PRs and eventually citizens, is that not a good outcome?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Rationally, one would think so but, of course, you can disagree.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In any case, we review our immigration policies regularly, to ensure that they remain relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If we come across good research that can help us in policy-thinking, we would certainly look into them deeply and welcome useful suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We can afford to remain selective as long as Singapore continues to be an attractive and welcoming place for immigrants.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, we cannot take for granted that this will always be so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must bear in mind this reality as we plan ahead, to secure a better future for current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do you have any clarifications, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira?
